rich_text.plain_text: Norway's abstract painters, when they arrived, did much the same. Jakob Weidemann (1923 to 2001) pioneered abstract painting in Norway in the decades after the Second World War, and his mature work gets described as abstract expressionism with nature as its basis. His best-known pictures are the skogbunnbilder, the forest floor paintings, shown at Kunstnernes Hus in Oslo in 1961: abstract, and also unmistakably a long look at the ground in a Norwegian wood. His contemporary Gunnar S. Gundersen (1921 to 1983) pushed nearer to pure form, debuting in 1947 and quickly counted among the leaders of abstract art in Norway, building his pictures out of flat fields of colour.

rich_text.plain_text: Painting's only half of it. Nordic abstraction had its widest life on cloth and paper. Maija Isola (1927 to 2001) made around 500 patterns for Marimekko across forty years, simple, bold, flat patterns printed at a dramatic scale, and her Unikko poppy of 1964 is the one everybody can picture: a flower cut back to a few flat shapes and blown up until the size does half the work. Marimekko's Finnish rather than Scandinavian strictly, but the instinct is regional. Reduce the motif, flatten the colour, repeat it.

rich_text.plain_text: The other thing behind the look is the stencil. A screenprint starts by cutting a shape out of paper, laying it over the mesh and pulling ink across it, and a cut edge can't describe anything: no modelling, no brushwork, no visible hand. It gives you silhouette, and then everything rests on whether the silhouette reads. Renate Thor still works this way, which is a large part of why her prints look the way they do.
